source: Battambang Provincial Department of Agriculture and the Cambodia Northwest Provinces Fruit Culture Development Committee (financial support from the SEILA Programme), Khmer translation of Photpeechon Whayooathdee, "ដំណាំខ្នុរ (Jackfruit)", "Translation Copy No. 4", January 1997 (500 copies printed). This is a Khmer translation of a Thai-language original: Whayooathdee, Photpeechon, "Jackfruit (2nd edition)", Nonthaburi Province, Thailand: Agriculture Lover's Printing House, 1988. Cover illustration source: Forestry/Fuelwood Research and Development Project, 1992, "Growing Multipurpose Trees on Small Farms", Winrock International, Bangkok. Other artwork by Sarath, Som, Center for Social Development, Phnom Penh, Dec. 1996.
text:
This is the longest chapter in the book (originally spanning book pages 12–26) and catalogs numerous named jackfruit varieties/types recognized in common usage, grouped broadly by fruit and flesh characteristics rather than strict cultivar pedigree. The chapter opens by explaining that jackfruit varieties are commonly distinguished first by flesh character — most importantly whether the ripe flesh is firm/crisp ("ជូតទិ" type, dry-fleshed) versus soft and very sweet/juicy ("ចួច" or soft-fleshed type) — a distinction the source treats as the single most practically important trait for buyers and growers because it determines how the fruit is eaten, stored, and sold.

Within this broad two-way split, the text describes and names a substantial number of locally recognized varieties, giving for several of them: approximate tree size and productivity (e.g., trees noted as bearing around 60–200 fruit per year in favorable conditions), typical fruit size and weight, rind spine density/sharpness, flesh color (ranging from pale yellow to deep orange), flesh thickness, seed size, and flavor/aroma notes (including some varieties noted for being notably fragrant, and others noted for having thinner or thicker flesh around the seed). The text also discusses that some named varieties are prized specifically for the vegetable/culinary use of their unripe fruit rather than for ripe eating quality, and that this is a separate axis of variety selection from ripe-fruit quality.

The chapter also touches on regional/named varieties tied to particular growers or localities (in the source's Thai-derived tradition, several varieties are named after the person or place that first propagated or popularized them), and notes that grafted/budded planting material from proven, high-yielding "mother trees" is the recommended way to reliably reproduce a desired variety's traits, since jackfruit grown from seed does not breed true and seedling trees vary widely in fruit quality, flesh type, and productivity compared to the parent tree.

Translation confidence note: many specific Khmer cultivar names in this chapter are transliterations of Thai variety names and could not all be read with full confidence from the scan; this summary intentionally describes the classification logic and general traits rather than asserting exact spellings of every named variety, to avoid misrepresenting names that were not clearly legible.
